title: Why is yawning contagious?
hook: Just reading about yawns can make you yawn. Science still isn’t sure why.
summary: There is no settled answer: contagion is strongest between people who are close, which hints at a link with empathy, but a large study found no such link.
cardText: Nobody knows for sure. Yawns spread most between relatives and friends, which hints at empathy, but a study of 328 people found no link with empathy at all.

cardBlocks.text: Seeing, hearing, reading or even thinking about a yawn can be enough to set your own jaw dropping. That is contagious yawning, different from the spontaneous kind that comes with boredom or tiredness. It isn’t only human: chimpanzees catch yawns too. In people, contagion is strongest between relatives, then friends, then acquaintances, and weakest between strangers. That is why it has been linked to empathy, the ability to share what others feel.

But the story doesn’t quite add up. In a Duke University study of 328 people, empathy didn’t predict who yawned; only age mattered, and even age explained just 8% of the differences. Another hypothesis says we simply pay more attention to familiar faces. For now, what contagious yawning is for remains unclear.
Yawns spread most between people who are close, but whether that comes from empathy is still debated.

deepDiveBlocks.text: We yawn spontaneously from the womb on, but contagious yawning only appears in childhood, around age 4 or 5. Something similar happens in chimpanzees: in a study of 33 orphaned chimps, juveniles caught human yawns, while infants were immune.

In a video experiment, two of six adult female chimpanzees yawned much more when they watched other chimps yawn. In another study, 21 of 29 dogs yawned after watching a person yawn, and none responded to mouth movements that weren’t yawns. The authors say human yawns are possibly contagious to dogs.

There are two main explanations for why contagion is stronger between people who are close. In the emotional hypothesis, it is a basic form of empathy, strongest with the people we love. In the attention hypothesis, we simply look more at familiar faces. One study looked only at yawns that could be heard but not seen, and contagion was still highest between friends and family, which supports the emotional hypothesis.

In the Duke study, volunteers watched a three-minute video of people yawning, and 222 of the 328 yawned at least once. Each person’s tendency was very stable from one test to the next. And most of those who didn’t yawn said they didn’t even feel the urge, so they weren’t holding back.
